name: CJC-1295 with DAC

lead: CJC-1295 with DAC is a long-acting analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). People use it in growth hormone peptide stacks hoping for a leaner, more muscular body, faster recovery and better-looking skin.

It mimics GHRH at the pituitary, and the DAC attachment binds blood proteins so its action lasts longer than the version without DAC. That sustained signal is meant to raise growth hormone output, which drives the body-composition payoff. Forum users debate pairing it with ipamorelin or tesamorelin versus choosing the no-DAC version; no trials have tested it for appearance.

paras: Users typically run it as one part of a growth hormone stack, paired with a growth hormone-releasing peptide such as ipamorelin or with tesamorelin. Forum threads mostly compare the DAC version with the shorter-acting no-DAC version. Posters describe changes in body composition, recovery and skin over weeks to months of use.

It is not an approved medicine, and risks in healthy users have not been defined by the sources available. Forum discussions focus on combinations rather than safety data, and products sold online are unregulated.

angle.text: CJC-1295 with DAC is a long-acting GHRH analogue that users stack with ipamorelin for a leaner, more muscular look, better recovery and skin. Sustained GHRH signalling is meant to raise growth hormone output, which feeds body composition. Its effects on appearance have not been tested in trials.

lead: CJC-1295 with DAC (also called DAC:GRF) is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) developed by ConjuChem Biotechnologies. A drug affinity complex (DAC) added to the peptide binds albumin in the blood, which extends how long it stays active compared with shorter-acting GHRH analogues such as the version without DAC (modified GRF 1-29).[1]

People in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities discuss it as a way to raise growth hormone (GH) and IGF-1 levels in pursuit of leaner, more muscular physiques, better sleep and recovery, and, among younger users, height and facial bone changes.[2][3] It is often described alongside ipamorelin or GHRPs such as GHRP-6, and sometimes tesamorelin.[4][5]

Wikipedia reports that in human subjects a single injection raised plasma GH two- to ten-fold for six days or longer and IGF-1 for roughly nine to eleven days, with an estimated half-life of about six to eight days.[1] It has not been approved as a medicine. Its development for lipodystrophy and GH deficiency reached phase II trials before being stopped after a participant died; the attending physician attributed the death to likely unrelated coronary disease, but the programme was ended as a precaution.[1]
infobox: CJC-1295 without DAC (modified GRF 1-29), tesamorelin, ipamorelin

paras: CJC-1295 is a modified form of GHRH (1-29) carrying a maleimidopropionyl lysine at the C-terminus that forms the drug affinity complex and binds albumin.[1] Wikipedia notes that CJC-1295 and modified GRF (1-29), also called CJC-1295 without DAC, are sometimes wrongly treated as the same compound in papers; the latter lacks the DAC group and has a much shorter duration of action.[1]

The peptide acts at the GHRH receptor on the pituitary to stimulate GH release, which in turn raises IGF-1. The DAC extension prolongs its presence in the bloodstream, so IGF-1 levels stay elevated for days to weeks after dosing.[1] Wikipedia reports elevated IGF-1 for up to 28 days after multiple doses.[1]

ConjuChem developed the compound for lipodystrophy and growth hormone deficiency, and it reached phase II clinical trials. The trial was discontinued after the death of a participant; the investigator's view was that the likely cause was asymptomatic coronary artery disease with plaque rupture and not the drug, but research was ended as a precaution.[1] It is not approved for medical use, and it is sold in the research-peptide market that forum users describe.

On looksmax.org, CJC-1295 with DAC appears in questions about peptide stacks, such as combining it with ipamorelin or tesamorelin. In one thread a user asked whether adding tesamorelin was dangerous; a reply argued there was no point in stacking several GHRH analogues and GHRPs and favoured the no-DAC version with ipamorelin.

Teenage users ask about the combination for height, sleep and facial bone growth, and ask whether growth plates would be affected; replies mostly redirect to HGH or dispute the height benefit.[2][3] Another user asked about pairing it with teriparatide.[6] On T Nation, older threads discuss it with GHRP-6 or modified GRF, and one 67-year-old poster described nightly ipamorelin and CJC-1295 with DAC as raising his IGF-1 from a very low level over three months.[4][5][7] These are anecdotes, and the wiki does not give dosing or sourcing instructions.

No studies found testing CJC-1295 with DAC for muscle, body composition or appearance. Early human pharmacology studies of the compound, cited by Wikipedia, measured GH and IGF-1 responses in healthy adults.[1] The phase II trial in lipodystrophy and GH deficiency was ended after one participant's death.[1]

lore.intro: CJC-1295 with DAC is discussed on looksmax.org and T Nation as a GH-boosting peptide, usually in stacks with ipamorelin or GHRPs.[4][7]

claims.claim: Using several GHRH analogues together gives a bigger result.
The no-DAC version with ipamorelin is preferable to the DAC version.
It can add height or facial bone growth in teenagers.
It restores low IGF-1 and improves recovery in older users.

timeline.event: ConjuChem develops DAC:GRF and runs early human pharmacology studies of GH and IGF-1 response.[1]
Phase II trial for lipodystrophy and GH deficiency stopped after a participant died.[1]
T Nation members discuss combining CJC-1295 forms with GHRP-6.[4][8]
